name: Nikhil Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good evening, Nikhil, and thanks for coming. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say is confidential and won't have your name on it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Okay with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, fine. I'll warn you, I don't know much about AI. I don't use any of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's completely fine. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do fit-out, mostly offices in the city centre, putting up partition walls and ceilings when a company refurbishes a floor. We work nights a lot because the offices are still in use during the day, so I start at six in the evening and finish around three in the morning. It's metal studs, plasterboard, screws, then the tapers come in to do the joints. I'm still rubbish at taping, Colm the supervisor always sends Ray to fix my bits, but I'm quick at boarding. I like the quiet at night, and the pay's better, but my sleep is a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most of this stuff is talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just say, told you, it's like those 3D TVs. Everyone said they'd change everything and now nobody's got one. Ray would agree with me, he thinks it's all nonsense too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing for me, and that's how I like it. I'd keep doing nights, keep learning to tape properly, and keep my money in the bank. I live with my parents, so I've got close to two years of wages saved, which sounds a lot but I've got nothing to spend it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same as now. Turn up, board, go home, sleep, five-a-side on Sundays. Maybe I'd finally put some of the savings towards a flat, because my mum keeps asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd maybe finally put the savings towards a flat. What's held you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't like big decisions. Signing papers for that much money makes me feel sick. My brother bought one and he's always moaning about repairs, so I keep thinking, why rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that's already changed because of technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawings are on a tablet now instead of paper, and Colm uses some app to order the boards. I don't touch it. If there's something on a screen I ask Ray, or I just wait till Colm tells me what to do.

S0.say: I'd say it was like those 3D TVs that were supposed to change everything. Ray would agree with me that it was all talk.
S0.think: It means nothing for me, which is how I like it. I live with my parents and have close to two years of wages saved, with nothing much to spend it on.
S0.do: Keeps doing the same night shifts, boarding and slowly learning to tape. Thinks about putting some savings toward a flat because his mum keeps asking, though he hasn't decided.
S0.quote: If there's something on a screen I ask Ray, or I just wait till Colm tells me what to do.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil is unbothered and avoids decisions, from flats to apps. His large cushion comes from living at home, not from a plan. He relies on colleagues to handle anything digital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many tasks in many jobs. Mine's not going to be one of the first, I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit offices way before it hits us. The people whose floors we're refurbishing are the ones who should worry. At work we'd probably joke that we'll be refitting their offices into robot rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. Every building's different, the walls aren't straight, the ceilings are full of old pipes, and you've got to work around people's stuff. I can't see a machine handling a 1970s office block at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really, for the first while. I'd wait and see what changes on our jobs, and if Colm says we're getting some new kit, I'd learn it when I have to. I'm not going on any course before someone tells me it's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little bit of 'hmm' in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'when I have to.' What would make you have to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Colm sat me down and said learn this or you're off the night crew. That's about it. If it's optional, I'd let the younger lads do it, even though I'm not that old myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the offices you refurbish. Have you noticed anything about those offices lately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actually, yeah. The last two jobs, the companies wanted fewer desks and more meeting rooms. One of the site managers said it's because half their staff aren't coming in anymore. So maybe the work changes even if we don't.

S1.say: I'd say it'll hit offices way before it hits builders. We'd joke that we'll be refitting their offices into robot rooms.
S1.think: I think I'm fine because every building's different, with crooked walls and old pipes. I can't see a machine handling a 1970s office block at two in the morning.
S1.do: Waits to see what changes on his jobs and does nothing new for the first while. Learns new kit only if his supervisor makes it a condition of staying on the night crew.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small doubt in the back of his head.
S1.quote: I can't see a machine handling a 1970s office block at two in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: He trusts the messiness of old buildings to protect him, which is a reasonable point for his kind of work. He'd only change under direct pressure from his supervisor. He spots on his own that office refurbishments are already changing shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots doing hands-on work in two years? I'd have to see that to believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's see it first. I'd say it at work and to my mates at football, because I honestly wouldn't believe it until a robot walked onto our site. I'm not really online, so I wouldn't say anything there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it's true, I'm in trouble, because I've got nothing else. I left school at fifteen and this is what I know. The good thing is I live at home and I've got the money, so I wouldn't be on the street, but I'd be twenty-nine with no job and no idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the flat, that's first, because I wouldn't want a mortgage with no job. I'd keep every penny in the bank and stop the stupid spending, the new trainers and that. And I'd lean on my parents, honestly, stay at home longer, help my dad at his shop if he needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel sick about it, but I'd know I wasn't going to go hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your dad's shop. Would that be work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's got a hardware shop on Station Road, screws, paint, keys cut. He's always saying I should come in with him. I always say no because it's boring, but if it came to it, I'd do it, even if robots probably come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep every penny in the bank. Have you thought about how long it would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. I'd guess years, because I don't pay rent. My mum would make me pay something, though, she's not soft.

S2.say: I'd say let's see it first, and I'd tell my mates I won't believe it until a robot walks onto our site. I wouldn't say anything online because I'm not really on there.
S2.think: If it's true I'm in trouble, because I left school at fifteen and this is all I know. I live at home with money saved, so I wouldn't be on the street, but I'd be twenty-nine with no job and no idea.
S2.do: Drops the idea of buying a flat and keeps all his savings in the bank. Cuts spending on things like new trainers, stays at his parents' home longer and would help at his dad's hardware shop if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious and a little sick about it, but sure he wouldn't go hungry.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-nine with no job and no idea.
S2.fieldNote: His first reaction is disbelief, then a frank admission that he has nothing else to fall back on but family. Living at home stops this tipping into alarm. He hasn't actually worked out how long his savings would last, which fits his avoidance of big decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same thing, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit easier to swallow. Still hard to believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, let's see it. Maybe I'd add that five years is a long time and loads can change. I'd still not believe it till I saw it on a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I'd probably think I've got time, which is the dangerous bit, because I'd use that as an excuse not to do anything. I know myself. I'd tell myself I'll sort it next year, every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, more than now, because I'd want a bigger pile if it really happens. I'd wait to see the first robots on jobs in the city before doing anything else. Maybe by year three, if I saw them, I'd ask my dad properly about the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit worried, but it's far enough away that I could switch it off most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save more. What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways after shift, that's a lot. We get food at four in the morning most nights, Ray and me, chicken shop by the station. That's probably a fortune over a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd tell yourself you'll sort it next year, every year. Is there anything that would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ray started doing something. Honestly. If my mate who's as stubborn as me went on some course, I'd think, right, it's serious.

S3.say: I'd still say let's see it, and that five years is a long time for things to change. I wouldn't believe it until I saw it on a real job.
S3.think: I'd think I've got time, which is dangerous because I'd use it as an excuse to do nothing. I'd tell myself I'll sort it next year, every year.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves more by cutting the late-night takeaways after shifts. Waits to see robots on city jobs, and if they appear by year three, asks his dad properly about joining the hardware shop.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off that he could switch it off most nights.
S3.quote: If my mate who's as stubborn as me went on some course, I'd think, right, it's serious.
S3.fieldNote: He's honest that more time would mainly give him more room to put things off. His real trigger for action is a peer, Ray, not news or policy. The chicken shop at four in the morning is a telling detail about his routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd have a bad back by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is ages, nobody knows what'll happen in ten years. I'd say it to anyone who brought it up. Probably by year eight I'd change my tune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same as the five-year one but even easier to ignore. I'd probably keep doing nights until my body tells me to stop. Maybe this would actually push me to buy the flat, because at least I'd own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and maybe finally get good at taping. I'd buy a flat in the next couple of years with my savings, something small I could rent out later if I needed the money. Beyond that, I'd wait and see what the world looks like in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's in the distance, like a dentist appointment in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would ten years push you to buy the flat, when two years made you drop the idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I'd have most of it paid off, or close to it. With two, I'd be stuck with a loan and no job. Bricks and mortar, my dad says, people always need somewhere to live, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your dad is right about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I'm not someone who reads about this. It's just the only advice I've ever been given about money, so I go with it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is ages and nobody knows what'll happen. I'd probably change my tune by year eight.
S4.think: It's even easier to ignore than the five-year one, and I'd keep doing nights until my body says stop. It might actually push me to buy the flat so I'd own something.
S4.do: Keeps doing his job and works on getting good at taping. Buys a small flat with his savings in the next couple of years that he could rent out later, and waits to see how things look in five years.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with the worry sitting in the distance like a dentist appointment in March.
S4.quote: Bricks and mortar, my dad says, people always need somewhere to live, robots or not.
S4.fieldNote: The warning time flips his decision about the flat, just as it did for spending. He follows his dad's single piece of money advice without testing it, and says so. The long timeline mostly gives him more room to wait.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to work out what else I could do and I've got nothing else. What would help is someone actually telling me what jobs are left and paying for me to learn one. Not a website, a person. I'm not going to figure it out on a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask Ray. He's worse than me with this stuff, and he's got a kid on the way.

headlineQuote: Not a website, a person. I'm not going to figure it out on a website.
portrait: Nikhil Lopez is a 27-year-old fit-out labourer who boards partition walls and ceilings on night shifts in city offices, still poor at taping but quick at boarding. He lives with his parents, has close to two years of wages saved, and avoids big decisions and anything on a screen. He shrugs off the milder pictures, trusting messy old buildings to protect him, and is anxious rather than alarmed in the fast AGI picture because his family home is a safety net. With more warning he admits he'd mostly wait, though ten years would push him to finally buy a flat on his dad's advice.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no time to work out what else he could do and has nothing else to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A real person telling him which jobs are left and paying for him to learn one, rather than a website.
